title: Do you have depression? A summative content analysis of mental health-related content on TikTok
screen_reason: Content analysis of the top 1,000 #mentalhealth TikTok videos (970 English-language analysed). Clinical experts judged every advice-and-information video as misleading / non-misleading, giving a quantitative share of items with a stated denominator: 33.0% (n = 106) of 319 advice videos were misleading. That is a share of items in a sample classified as misleading, i.e. CONTENT.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language TikTok videos; author team Canada/USA)
estimates.measure_type: % of mental-health advice/information TikTok videos judged misleading by clinical experts
estimates.value_raw: misleading in 33.0% (n = 106) of videos; non-misleading in 67.0% (n = 215)
estimates.denominator: 319 of the 970 analysed English-language videos that were coded as offering mental-health advice and information (drawn from the top 1,000 most-viewed #mentalhealth videos)
estimates.definition: A video whose advice/information was labelled 'misleading' by clinical experts — either containing overtly inaccurate facts, or lacking sufficient context and so risking inappropriate conclusions or self-diagnosis
estimates.misinfo_def: "Authors JS and RS viewed each video and determined whether its content was misleading, non-misleading, or unable to determine"; misleading videos "contained overtly inaccurate facts; others lacked sufficient context to make conclusions and risked leading to inappropriate conclusions or self-diagnoses"
estimates.source_quote: advice given was coded as non-misleading in 67.0% ( n  = 215) of videos and misleading in 33.0% ( n  = 106).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Advice and information' subsection; sample described in Table 1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Second coding team of clinical experts — one licensed clinical psychologist (JS) and two psychiatrists (SM, RS). Two coders independently labelled each advice video misleading / non-misleading / unable to determine; the third broke ties. True disagreement in 23.1% (n = 74) of videos, one 'unable to determine' label in a further 26.5% (n = 85); 72.3% agreement reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: We collected the top 1000 videos with the most views on TikTok (desktop version) with the hashtag #mentalhealth from October 12 to October 16, 2021. … Only videos in English were included, resulting in a final sample of 970 videos. … A second coding team of clinical experts, consisting of a licensed clinical psychologist (JS) and two psychiatrists (SM, RS) were involved in assessing the quality and accuracy of videos giving advice and information (n = 319).
estimates.notes: borderline=true on the CONTENT/QUALITY line. The label is an explicit expert misleading/non-misleading judgement (which the rules put under CONTENT), but part of the operational criterion is insufficient context rather than falsity — a wholly accurate but incomplete video could be labelled misleading, which pulls towards QUALITY. Coded CONTENT because the judgement is substantive expert verification of accuracy, not a DISCERN/GQS/JAMA-style completeness instrument; flagged for adjudication. Denominator is the advice subset (319), not the full 970, so this is NOT a prevalence of misinformation across #mentalhealth content. NUMERIC INCONSISTENCY in the paper: 106 + 215 = 321, but the advice theme is reported as n = 319 in Table 1 and in the methods; 33.0% is consistent with a 321 denominator (106/321 = 33.02%). The stated 33.0% is kept verbatim per R8. Sample is the top-1,000 most-viewed hashtag videos, hence denom_selection=curated. Agreement on the underlying advice theme itself was only 78.4%, below the study's own 80% threshold.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Creator-type split: HCPs 24.6% misleading (n = 61 videos), non-HCPs 35.0% misleading (n = 260). Not extracted as separate rows — these are creator subgroups, not the paper's headline, and the rule is to keep the main figure. An adjudicator may wish to add them if creator type is treated like a party/partisan headline split. (2) Theme prevalences (personal story 59.1%, advice 32.9%, emoting 20.4%, death 13.2%, science 3.8%, product 1.6%) are topical content categories, not veracity judgements — no rows. (3) Engagement figures (Table 1, Figure 1: misleading content performed better on views/likes/comments/shares) are not reported as a share of exposure attributable to misleading videos, and the split totals needed for one are not given, so no EXPOSURE or CONCENTRATION row is derivable without computing a cross-category quantity (forbidden by R8). (4) Misinformation percentages for other conditions (47–90%; ADHD 51%) are figures the paper cites from other studies — excluded per R8.

rob.design: Cross-sectional summative content analysis. Frame: top 1,000 most-viewed TikTok videos carrying #mentalhealth, scraped 12–16 October 2021 (desktop); 30 non-English videos removed leaving 970. No probability sampling, no response rate (non-survey). Six-member coding team applied a pilot-tested coding frame; a separate team member audited all coding; all codes reached ≥80% agreement except the advice/information theme at 78.4%. Accuracy judgements made by three clinicians with tie-breaking; 72.3% agreement, 23.1% true disagreements, 26.5% involving an 'unable to determine' label. Authors note the top-listed hashtag frame and English-only restriction as limitations.
rob.item6_quote: Authors JS and RS viewed each video and determined whether its content was misleading, non-misleading, or unable to determine, and labeled them accordingly.
rob.item10_quote: After resolving any coder disagreement, advice given was coded as non-misleading in 67.0% (n = 215) of videos and misleading in 33.0% (n = 106).
